title: Early dopamine elevation modifies the behavioral consequences of maternal separation in female and male juvenile mice
authors: Reis, A. L. d. A. L.; Valverde, P. B.; Avritzer, S. C.; Guerra, L. T. L.; Resende, B. L.; Moraes, M. A.; Arabe, L. B.; Mourao, F. A. G.; Moraes, M. F. D.; Souza, R. P.; Souza, B. R.
abstract: Alterations in dopaminergic signaling and exposure to early-life stress are both implicated in the developmental origins of psychiatric disorders, yet little is known about how these factors interact during sensitive periods of brain maturation. We investigated whether increased dopamine availability during early postnatal development modifies the behavioral consequences of maternal separation in female and male C57BL/6 mice. From postnatal day (PD) 1 to PD14, mice received L-Dopa plus benserazide, maternal separation (3 h/day), their combination, or the corresponding control conditions. We assessed mice behavior between PD28 and PD32 using novel object recognition, open-field, elevated plus-maze, marble-burying, and forced-swim tests, followed by hippocampal volumetric analysis. Early L-Dopa exposure produced sex- and behavior-specific effects. In females, L-Dopa increased rearing without altering horizontal locomotion and modified open-arm exploration and stress-coping behavior, whereas in males it increased open-arm exploration and reduced climbing frequency. Maternal separation produced distinct effects in females and males and reduced repetitive digging/burying behavior in both sexes. Importantly, maternal separation frequently modified rather than potentiated the effects of L-Dopa. In both sexes, combined maternal separation and L-Dopa opposed several L-Dopa-associated alterations in open-field, elevated plus-maze, and forced-swim behaviors. Recognition memory was largely preserved across experimental conditions. L-Dopa also reduced hippocampal volume selectively in females, whereas hippocampal volume was higher in females exposed to maternal separation plus L-Dopa than in those receiving L-Dopa alone. Multivariate analyses revealed overlapping rather than treatment-specific behavioral clusters, indicating substantial individual heterogeneity and sex-dependent shifts in multidimensional behavioral profiles. Together, these findings demonstrate that transient alterations in dopamine availability and maternal separation interact non-additively during early postnatal development. Their consequences depend on sex, behavioral domain, and developmental timing, supporting a model in which neurochemical and environmental perturbations dynamically shape behavioral trajectories rather than simply producing cumulative developmental damage.

title: Spontaneous Hemodynamic Oscillations during Sleep Coordinate Directional CSF Flow in the Subarachnoid Space and Ventricles
authors: Chen, D.; Wang, F.; Strom, A.; Yun, H.; Polimeni, J. R.; Dong, Z.; Lewis, L. D.
abstract: During sleep, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow is enhanced and thought to facilitate clearance of metabolic waste from the brain. Human imaging has shown that sleep is associated with large waves of bulk CSF flow in the fourth ventricle; however, the CSF flow dynamics around brain tissue are unknown. Here, we investigated how CSF flow is organized across the subarachnoid space, a key site both for fluid exchange across cortical surface and for transport out of the cranium. We used an MRI technology at 7 Tesla that simultaneously measures cortical hemodynamics and slow subarachnoid CSF flow and applied this during sleep. We found that spontaneous infraslow hemodynamic oscillations were coupled to spatially structured, directional CSF flow throughout both ventricular and subarachnoid compartments. Hemodynamic oscillations and fourth-ventricle bulk flow were both associated with brain-wide CSF flow at different phases, indicating that they reflect a single coordinated CSF movement cycle. Compared to cardiac pulsations, a canonical driver of CSF movement, hemodynamic-driven CSF flow showed a distinct directional pattern and was smaller in instantaneous amplitude but produced substantially greater cumulative displacement and thus greater potential for transport within an oscillation period. Together, these findings show that hemodynamic oscillations during sleep are coupled to temporally coordinated and directional CSF flow throughout the ventricles and subarachnoid space, suggesting that sleep-dependent neuronal activity drives fluid movement across the human brain in a distinct spatial pattern.

title: Co-option of CENP-A for activity-induced neuronal plasticity
authors: Stankovic, A.; Gonzalez-Bohorquez, D.; Mallona, I.; Quiniou, M.; Jaeger, B.; Korobeynyk, V.; Brandi, L.; Guenther, S.; Ruenker, A.; Garthe, A.; Cruz Ochoa, N.; Foldy, C.; Furlan, S.; Kempermann, G.; Robinson, M. D.; Jessberger, S.
abstract: Neuronal activation drives activity-dependent gene expression that underlies experience-associated synaptic modifications, learning and memory. Here we show that the histone variant CENP-A, best known for specifying centromere identity, is dynamically regulated by synaptic activity at both the RNA and protein levels in postmitotic neurons. Neuronal activation increases a non-centromeric nuclear pool of CENP-A while leaving centromeric CENP-A levels unchanged. Downregulation of CENP-A selectively reduces the activity-associated non-centromeric pool, impairs activity-dependent induction of immediate-early genes such as FOS and ARC, and disrupts hippocampus-dependent learning and memory. Furthermore, we find that activity-dependent neuronal responses in human embryonic stem cell-derived forebrain organoids similarly require CENP-A. Our results reveal a mitosis-independent, conserved role of CENP-A for driving plasticity in mammalian neurons.

title: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is associated with defective membrane repair and dysregulation of annexin-A1/A2 in skeletal muscle
authors: Le Quang, M.; d'Agata, L.; Carmeille, R.; Rassinoux, P.; Ruiz, J.; Koenig, C.; Gounou, C.; Salesses, A.; Bouvet, F.; Mamchaoui, K.; Dovero, S.; Deburgrave, N.; Leturcq, F.; Juban, G.; Sole, G.; Martin-Negrier, M.-L.; Bouter, A.
abstract: Background: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is caused by mutations in the DMD gene, which encodes dystrophin in skeletal muscle cells. Despite extensive knowledge of dystrophin function, the cellular mechanisms responsible for progressive muscle degeneration remain poorly understood. Methods: We investigated sarcolemma integrity, membrane repair capacity, and annexin protein expression in DMD patient muscle biopsies and human skeletal muscle cell lines using immunohistochemistry, both shear stress-based and laser irradiation injury assays, Western blotting, and live-cell imaging of GFP-tagged annexins. To assess whether extracellular annexin A2 (ANXA2) is associated with disease severity, we further analyzed muscle biopsies from patients with Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD) and compared the mdx and D2-mdx mouse models. Results: We identified defective membrane repair in DMD skeletal muscle cells, independent of increased membrane fragility, by evaluating resealing capacity in control and DMD patient-derived cell lines using both a shear stress assay (N = 12, p < 0.0001) and a laser irradiation assay (N = 3, p < 0.0001). Analyses performed on human DMD muscle biopsies (N = 10) further confirmed this defect, demonstrating massive intracellular IgG uptake (p < 0.0001) together with altered annexin expression profiles. While mechanical stress induces the upregulation of annexin A5 (ANXA5, p < 0.01) and A6 (ANXA6, p < 0.05) in healthy skeletal muscle cells - suggesting an adaptive response to membrane damage - we observed dysregulated expression patterns of these proteins in DMD cells. Notably, ANXA1 (p < 0.05) and ANXA2 (p < 0.01) were not only significantly overexpressed but also aberrantly localized to the extracellular space, a putative consequence of defective membrane repair. Importantly, extracellular ANXA2 was progressively increased with disease severity, showing intermediate levels in BMD (N = 3, p < 0.05) compared with DMD biopsies and greater accumulation in D2-mdx than in mdx mice (N = 3, p < 0.05), identifying extracellular ANXA2 as a marker closely associated with dystrophinopathy severity. Conclusions: Our findings identify defective membrane repair as a central pathogenic mechanism in human DMD and indicate that the extracellular accumulation of ANXA2 results from impaired membrane repair and is associated with disease severity. Together, these findings suggest that extracellular annexins may contribute to disease progression and represent potential therapeutic targets, provided that their extracellular functions can be selectively inhibited without compromising their essential intracellular role in membrane repair.

title: Analysis of ribosomes from the Wild-type and FMR1 knockout human embryonic stem cells
authors: Kharbanda, T.; D'Souza, M. N.; Palakodeti, D.; Muddashetty, R. S.; Kutti, V. R.
abstract: Fragile X Messenger Ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMRP) is a multifunctional, multidomain RNA-binding protein whose loss causes Fragile X syndrome. It is also known to associate with ribosomes and modulate translation. In human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), knockout (KO) of the FMR1 gene results in significantly increased protein translation rates and alterations in the 2'-O-methylation patterns of rRNA. To understand the structural underpinnings of the process, we performed structural analysis of ribosomes isolated from both the wild-type (WT) and the FMR1 KO hESCs, which revealed populations of ribosomes with distinct protein factors and tRNA in the FMR1 KO ribosome preparations. The bound protein factors are hallmarks of dormant ribosomes, which are currently not observed in the WT hESCs, and are characterized by the binding of SERPINE-mRNA binding protein 1 in the mRNA tunnel and eukaryotic elongation factor 2 near the A-site. The observation of elevated protein translation in FMR1 KO cells, alongside a subpopulation of dormant ribosomes, further substantiates the role of FMRP in translational regulation. Additionally, we analysed the 2'-O-methylation patterns in the 28S rRNA, in both the WT and the FMR1 KO hESCs, identifying a few potential differentially methylated sites. Thus, these observations provide insights into the mechanisms of ribosome dormancy in the absence of FMRP and in understanding the role of rRNA methylation in translational regulation.

title: Calibrated analysis framework for nanopore direct RNA sequencing uncovers cell-specific m6A proportions at conserved sites
authors: Ohnezeit, D.; Loliashvili, E.; Putzel, G.; Verstraten, R.; Silhavy, A. T.; Liu, J.; Nicholson, L. S.; Pironti, A.; Jaffrey, S. R.; Depledge, D. P.; Wilson, A. C.
abstract: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) coupled with Dorado modification-aware basecalling enables mapping of epitranscriptomic modifications including N6-methyladenosine (m6A) at the level of individual RNAs. However, the sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility of this method remain unclear and have only recently begun to be addressed through systematic benchmarking studies. Here, we aimed to establish a best-practice workflow for DRS-based epitranscriptomic analyses. Specifically, we evaluated multiple Dorado versions and models using RNA isolated from primary cells and unmodified in vitro transcribed RNAs. We further utilized an m6A methyltransferase inhibitor as a specificity control. We established that stringent filtering is necessary to reduce the contribution of background and found that Dorado predictions captured an increasing proportion of GLORI sites detected at high m6A/A proportions. Further, by applying DRS to a human primary fibroblast and a HD10.6 neuron dataset, we detected differences in the predicted m6A/A proportions at conserved sites between these datasets. Our study thus presents the first systematic comparison of Dorado and GLORI from the same input RNA and expands characterization of the m6A epitranscriptome to fibroblasts and neurons.

title: KRAS recognition by Src: Mechanistic insights from Molecular Dynamics Simulations
authors: Lu, H.; Xu, H.; Marti, J.; Ma, B.; FARAUDO, J.
abstract: c-Src, the first identified oncogene, and Ras, one of the most frequently mutated proteins in human cancers, can activate each other to promote tumorigenesis. Recent experimental work has found that c-Src can recognize and phosphorylate both GTP-bound and GDP-bound forms of KRas, as well as GTP-bound NRas and GDP-bound HRas. The molecular mechanisms underlying this specific recognition remain unknown. We leverage molecular simulation tools (eg. Molecular dynamics and Markov State Models analysis) to model a Src-KRas interaction in solution to identify the mechanisms underlying the c-Src recognition of the G12D mutant of KRas4B-G12D, the most prevalent in humans. We found that the most populated states of nucleotide-bound KRas maintain more open and dynamic switch regions, facilitating easier access of c-Src to the phosphorylation sites of KRas (Tyr32 for GTP-bound KRas and Tyr64 for GDP-bound KRas). We further identify two c-Src specific regions (residues 340-359 and 453-473), along with putative recognition hotspots at Leu347, Asp348, Lys351, Gly459, Arg460, and Val461, that may contribute to the stabilization of phosphorylation-competent KRas conformations. c-Src selectively recognizes and engages specific macrostates of KRas, which may constitute privileged targets for the rational design of peptide-based inhibitors.

title: Virtual Brain Modelling Reveals Altered Network Dynamics and Predicts Symptom Severity in Schizophrenia: Relevance to Antipsychotic Treatment Response and Resistance.
authors: Vitacca, M.; Pischedda, D.; Ciccarelli, M.; Pontillo, G.; De Simone, G.; Cocozza, S.; Cipranic, F.; Monteverdi, A.; Fusar-Poli, P.; Gandini Wheeler-Kingshott, C. A. M.; Palesi, F.; de Bartolomeis, A.; D'Angelo, E.
abstract: Background: Schizophrenia (SZ) is a heterogeneous disorder characterized by positive, negative, cognitive and disorganisation symptoms, with pleomorphic phenotype and poorly understood aetiology. Dopamine dysregulation represents the most replicated in vivo pathophysiology finding. However, accumulating evidence suggests altered large-scale brain connectivity and excitation/inhibition balance disruption. While quantifying these alterations would help clarify SZ neurophysiology and guide therapy, single-patient identification remains impractical. This is particularly relevant for treatment-resistant SZ (TRS) whose pathophysiology remains unclear. Methods: Using virtual brain modelling, we simulated large-scale brain dynamics from functional and structural MRI data in 43 healthy controls and 33 SZ patients, stratified into TRS and non-TRS. We used the Wong-Wang model to derive four network parameters reflecting GABAergic and NMDA receptor-mediated glutamatergic transmission: global coupling (G), local inhibitory (Ji) and excitatory (JNMDA) coupling, and recurrent excitation (w+). We performed simulations in the whole brain and in resting-state networks, compared model parameters between groups and tested their association with Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) scores. Results: Compared to non-TRS, TRS patients showed increased JNMDA and decreased w+ at the whole-brain level, increased JNMDA and G in the dorsal attention network, lower G in the limbic network and increased w+ in the visual network. Moreover, Ji in the default mode network predicted negative symptom severity while JNMDA in the limbic and ventral attention networks predicted total PANSS scores and disorganisation. Conclusions: These findings suggest that TRS is characterized by network-specific alterations in excitation/inhibition profiles and support the use of personalised multiscale modelling to identify symptom biomarkers.

title: Sequential Sampling as a Computational Principle of Episodic Memory
authors: Kerren, C.; Dixit, S.; Coxon, E.; Nikolaev, A. R.; Doeller, C. F.
abstract: Visual perception unfolds through sequential eye movements, yet computational models of episodic memory typically assume that event representations already exist. Here, we propose that sequential gaze sampling does not simply supply memory with visual information, but contributes to the construction and organisation of episodic representations. We introduce a computational model in which successive fixations are integrated into an evolving internal representation, subsequently stored in associative memory and later retrieved through partial reinstatement of the original sampling trajectory. Within to-be-remembered elements, successive samples support progressive individuation; between elements, more frequent transitions strengthen relational binding. As sampling proceeds, internal representations become progressively lower-dimensional while retaining information about where samples were taken and when they occurred in the sequence. Sampling history also remains embedded in the resulting representation: changing the order of otherwise identical samples alters both the representation itself and element-specific retrieval. At retrieval, reinstating more of the original sampling trajectory improves access to specific elements, while competition is strongest when memories share both semantic category and sampling history. Finally, an exploratory generative readout shows that regions sampled during encoding are reconstructed more faithfully than unsampled regions. Together, these findings suggest that sequential sampling provides a candidate computational process through which episodic representations are constructed, shaping their subsequent storage and retrieval.

title: Human Hippocampal Theta-Gamma Phase-Amplitude Coupling Signals the Distance to Remembered Goals
authors: Huang, Z.; Goumas, P.; Bisby, J. A.; Rodionov, R.; Diehl, B.; McEvoy, A. W.; Walker, M. C.; Vivekananda, U.; Burgess, N.; Bush, D.
abstract: In mammals, flexible navigation is believed to rely on a cognitive map of known locations supported by the hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal lobe structures. Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit spatial firing fields within a given environment. Moreover, their firing is modulated by the movement-related theta rhythm such that "theta sweeps" of place cell activity encode the trajectory towards a hidden reward location during goal-directed navigation. Here, we attempted to detect signatures of theta sweeps in the human hippocampal local field potential (LFP) recorded with intracranial EEG. Specifically, we hypothesised that sequences of locations along a planned trajectory encoded by distinct cell assemblies are associated with gamma activity at successive theta phases. To test this hypothesis, we asked N=9 patients with epilepsy to perform a spatial navigation task in desktop virtual reality while we recorded LFP signals from depth electrode contacts implanted across the medial temporal lobe. Consistent with our predictions, we found an increase in hippocampal theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, a decrease in gamma power, and theta phase precession of gamma activity as hidden goal locations were approached and the sequence of locations remaining to be traversed became shorter. This suggests that goal-directed hippocampal theta sweeps during navigation are reflected in LFP theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, and that these neural mechanisms of model-based planning are conserved across species.

title: The Role of Locus Coeruleus and Substantia Nigra/Ventral Tegmental Area activity in Reward and Salience Processing: A High-Resolution fMRI Study
authors: Hall, J. M.; Kukkonen, N.; Prinea, E.; Schomaker, J.; Krebs, R. M.
abstract: Dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra/ventral tegmental area (SN/VTA) are classically associated with reward processing, whereas noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus (LC) have been shown to support salience processing more broadly. However, rewarding stimuli are also inherently salient, and in most paradigms reward and salience are conflated, for example when rewarded targets are also rare and/or visually distinct. As a result, it remains unclear in how far these systems are sensitive to reward-specific properties or more basic salient properties of the stimulus. Using a visual oddball paradigm with high-resolution fMRI (n = 45), we compared oddballs that were rewarded, visually salient, or neutral, while keeping stimulus probability and motor requirements constant across conditions. Participants responded more accurately to rewarded than to neutral oddballs, and faster to rewarded than to both neutral and visually salient oddballs. At the neural level, SN/VTA activity was increased for rewarded oddballs compared with both neutral and visually salient oddballs, whereas LC activity was increased for rewarded compared with visually salient oddballs. Visual salience alone did not increase activity in either region relative to neutral oddballs. Together, these findings suggest that both the noradrenergic and dopaminergic systems are preferentially engaged by motivationally relevant stimuli, beyond more basic forms of salience.

title: Neural abstraction of evidence accumulation enables flexible multidimensional perceptual decisions
authors: Benjamin, L.; Drevet, J.; Wyart, V.
abstract: Human perceptual decisions adapt to rich and changing contexts but are typically tested under impoverished conditions. To probe this flexibility, we examined decisions requiring both the selection and the combination of multiple sensory features across sequences of objects. Here we show that human decision flexibility extends beyond feature selection to combination, even across sensory modalities, supported by the abstraction of underlying neural representations. Rapid magnetoencephalographic (MEG) responses reveal a hierarchy of object representations that become increasingly abstract and gated according to their decision relevance. A shared abstract representation of updates reflects evidence accumulation collapsed onto the relevant axis across unidimensional (selection-based) and multidimensional (combination-based) contexts. Recurrent neural networks tested under the same conditions acquire and benefit from abstract representations only when operating under human levels of computational noise. Together, these findings provide a flexibility through abstraction account of human decisions across a broader range of everyday perceptual conditions.

title: Independently tunable subcortical oscillators enable prefrontal control of cortical coupling
authors: Mozaffarilegha, M.; Kolaxi, A.; Nikoletopoulou, V.; Ito, H. T.
abstract: Oscillatory coherence between brain regions varies flexibly with behavioral demands, yet the circuit mechanism underlying this control remains unclear. Theta rhythm, which coordinates prefrontal-hippocampal activity, is classically attributed to a pacemaker in the medial septum (MS), with the supramammillary nucleus (SuM) as its modulator. Here we show that SuM instead operates as an independently tunable theta oscillator. In rats performing a spatial alternation task, SuM theta frequency decreased before the choice point while MS theta frequency remained stable, reducing the SuM-MS frequency mismatch in both population spiking and local field potentials. The size of this mismatch predicted theta-rhythm coordination between the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and hippocampal CA1 in both the alternation task and open-field foraging. Inhibiting direct mPFC input to SuM abolished the behavior-dependent modulation of SuM frequency and disrupted mPFC-CA1 coupling. These findings place a subcortical theta oscillator under top-down prefrontal control and identify the SuM-MS frequency mismatch as a control variable for interregional coordination.

title: A gαq signaling pathway in dopaminergic neurons suppresses memory
authors: Martinez-Cervantes, J. C.; Shah, P.; Cervantes Sandoval, I.
abstract: Which experiences persist as memories is a fundamental question in neurobiology. The balance between memory persistence and suppression is thought to be optimal for an organism to adapt to the ever-changing environment. Memory suppression is a process by which the brain limits the strength and expression of memories. Memory suppressors are genes whose disruption can enhance memory at different stages: acquisition, consolidation, forgetting, or recall. Here, using aversive classical conditioning in Drosophila, we show that Gq acts as a memory suppressor in PPL1 dopaminergic neurons. Knockdown of gq in dopaminergic neurons enhances acquisition, strengthens anesthesia-resistant memory, and impairs reversal learning. In vivo functional imaging revealed that gq knockdown amplifies shock-evoked responses in a type of PPL1 neuron. Additionally, using ex vivo imaging and pharmacological experiments, we reveal that both Gq and the OAMB receptor alter octopamine-evoked ER calcium responses in PPL1 neurons. Our results uncover a new role of Gq signaling within dopaminergic neurons that suppresses memory.

title: Nicotinic control of dopamine release shapes striatal output and engages adaptive action selection.
authors: Guven, E. B.; Kocaturk, S.; Shiflett, M.; Assous, M.
abstract: Acetylcholine and dopamine significantly modulate striatal circuits and are essential for reward learning and action selection. Cholinergic interneurons can locally trigger dopamine release through beta2-containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptors expressed on dopamine axons1-3. However, the causal contribution of this local cholinergic control of dopamine to behaviour and striatal output remains unresolved, with recent studies reaching contrasting conclusions about the extent and behavioural relevance of local acetylcholine-dopamine coupling4-6. Here, to directly test the causal contribution of this pathway, we conditionally deleted beta2-containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptors from midbrain neurons in adult mice. This manipulation selectively abolished cholinergic interneuron-evoked dopamine release in the striatum. In a reward-based instrumental task, mice lacking this pathway showed decrements in effort that depended on the reinforcement context, and failed to adjust actions in a choice task when effort and reward costs varied. Substantia nigra beta2-containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptor deletion also markedly weakened cholinergic interneuron-mediated disynaptic inhibition of striatal projection neurons, showing that disruption of beta2-dependent cholinergic control of dopamine alters how cholinergic activity is transmitted to striatal output. Together, these findings establish the importance of local acetylcholine-dopamine coupling for regulating striatal output and influencing whether actions are sustained and adjusted as effort, reward, and outcomes change.

title: Development of a genetically encoded fluorescent indicator for monitoring GPR52 activation
authors: Lan, G.; Wang, H.; Qian, T.; Xie, S.; Qian, C.; Ursu, D.; Bornemann, K. D.; Hengerer, B.; Li, Y.
abstract: GPR52 is an orphan G protein-coupled receptor implicated in psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders, but its endogenous ligand remains unidentified, limiting the exploration of its physiological functions and therapeutic potential. We pioneered a novel methodology for orphan GPCR ligand discovery utilizing the GPCR-activation-based (GRAB) strategy by developing GPR52-1.0, a genetically encoded fluorescent sensor. GPR52-1.0 exhibits excellent membrane trafficking and high sensitivity in HEK293T cells, cultured neurons, and acute mouse brain slices. Notably, it detects neuronal activity-dependent endogenous ligand release in the striatum, with responses abolished by a specific antagonist. This sensor provides a powerful tool for identifying GPR52's endogenous ligand(s) and enables real-time monitoring of its activation. Our work lays the foundation for uncovering GPR52's physiological roles and supports future efforts to develop GPR52-targeted therapeutics.

title: Decoding super-enhancer regulatory grammar and pathogenic gain-of-function variants directly from DNA sequence
authors: Liang, Y.; Xu, X.; Mao, Y.; Zheng, Z.; Liu, N.
abstract: Super-enhancers (SEs) drive cell-identity gene expression, yet their identification relies on epigenomic profiling (e.g., H3K27ac ChIP-seq), precluding discovery in unprofiled cellular states and leaving their underlying sequence grammar unknown. Here, we present Borzoi-SE, a deep learning framework built upon the genomic transformer Borzoi that formulates SE discovery as hierarchical, cell-type-resolved genomic object detection directly from long-range sequence across 90 human lineages. Base-resolution attribution recovers lineage-defining master transcription factors across cell types. Within SEs shared across lineages, it reveals lineage-dependent motif usage, suggesting that the same regulatory regions can support distinct cell-type-specific programs. Using in silico ablation, Borzoi-SE decoded the functional hierarchy of the {beta}-globin super-enhancer, prioritizing hypersensitive site 2 (HS2) as the dominant constituent, which we experimentally verified via CRISPR interference. Trained without variant-effect labels, Borzoi-SE identified gain-of-super-enhancer variants in different tissues. At the CHRM2 locus, a single-nucleotide variant created a de novo glucocorticoid receptor (GR) motif that recruited activated GR and potentiated adjacent MEF2 regulatory syntax, nucleating a cardiac super-enhancer. Orthogonal multi-omics and population-genetic evidence linked this variant to increased CHRM2 expression and variation in resting heart rate and PR-interval duration. Borzoi-SE establishes a general framework for decoding SE regulatory grammar and prioritizing causal non-coding variants directly from sequence.

title: scMTG reconstructs single-cell temporal dynamics with Markov transition generators
authors: Cui, X.; Wang, H.; Gao, Z.; Jiang, R.; Wong, W. H.; Liu, Q.
abstract: Single-cell time-series data offer a unique opportunity to study how cell states emerge, evolve, and diversify over time. However, cells are destructively measured across time points and individual cells cannot be directly tracked, making it challenging to reconstruct cell-state transitions and uncover the dynamic regulatory programs. Existing methods are predominantly based on optimal transport and typically require predefined low-dimensional representations, which can limit scalability, flexibility, and mechanistic interpretability. Here we present scMTG, a single-cell Markov transition generative framework that jointly learns cell representations and temporal cell-state transitions from unpaired single-cell time-series data. In a series of experiments, scMTG demonstrates superior performance in interpolating held-out missing-time-point data and inferring cross-time-point transition matrices, compared with state-of-the-art methods. More importantly, the learned Markov transition generator provides an interpretable framework for identifying the molecular programs that drive cell-state changes, enabling characterization of cell fate decisions and construction of time-resolved regulatory networks. Together, scMTG provides a unified generative framework for reconstructing cellular dynamics and uncovering regulatory programs that shape development, differentiation, and disease progression. scMTG is available as open-source software at https://github.com/liuq-lab/scMTG.

title: Joint Variable Selection for Omic Biomarkers in Time-to-Event Data
authors: Bajzik, J.; Depope, A.; Zolfimoselo, Y.; Sharipov, A.; Lesayova, A.; Klein, H.; Richmond, A.; Vernardis, S.; Grauslys, A.; Andrejev, S.; Zelezniak, A.; Ralser, M.; Marioni, R.; Mondelli, M.; Robinson, M. R.
abstract: The incidence of the vast majority of neurodegenerative, cancer, and metabolic diseases generally increases exponentially with age. In large-scale biobanks, linking time-to-diagnosis information in electronic health records to multiple genomic (``multiomics'') measures has the potential to reveal the genes and biological pathways involved in the disease onset and progression. To date, association testing has commonly been conducted by testing one variable at a time using semiparametric Cox proportional hazards (CoxPH) models, which ignores correlation structure and increases the risk of false discoveries. To address these issues, we introduce a novel fully parametric Bayesian computational method, vampW, based on the Vector Approximate Message Passing framework applied to a Weibull model. vampW jointly models correlated features, while providing an interpretable hazard structure, producing a continuous survival curve, and incorporating prior knowledge. In an extensive simulation study, we demonstrate that joint modeling of omics data and time-to-event outcomes with vampW, substantially reduces false discoveries in comparison to marginal testing and other forms of joint CoxPH models. In 53,018 individuals from the UK Biobank, vampW identifies 219 protein associations with 24 disease outcomes, most of which are not among the top marginal discoveries. We further correct protein levels for exponential age effects, identifying 1,308 associations and highlighting the sensitivity of the analysis to age-correction methodology. Our findings replicate in independent cohorts using different measurement technologies, within data from Iceland and a novel Generation Scotland proteomics dataset. vampW also achieves significant improvement in the prediction of disease onset times: across 14 outcomes, it reduces the root mean squared error by over 30% and 26%, when compared to CoxPH variants and the deep learning approach DeepSurv, respectively, while maintaining predictive utility in minority populations. In summary, vampW offers accurate and interpretable variable selection and out-of-sample prediction within a single computational framework, making it a powerful tool for dissecting the genomic architecture of common complex disease onset.

title: Multivalent Surface Search Dynamics Shape Bacteriophage Adsorption Efficiency: A Stochastic Model of Tail Fiber Optimization
authors: Yadav, A.; Sneppen, K.; Mitarai, N.
abstract: Phages must locate and bind to bacterial surface receptors to initiate infection. Their tail fiber configuration critically influences this process. We develop a stochastic model describing surface search as a renewal process, incorporating attachment, detachment, and target-finding steps. Using both numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we quantify how tail fiber number, attachment-detachment rates, and geometric constraints impact the mean and the distribution of time to successful adsorption. Notably, the search efficiency shows a nonmonotonic dependence on tail fiber number, governed by a trade-off between binding stability and diffusion-mediated mobility. This optimum shifts depending on the effective bacterial density, target radius, and fiber reach. Short fiber reach imposes severe geometric constraints, reducing mobility at high tail fiber counts and leading to performance degradation. Our findings suggest that phage adsorption strategies are shaped by a balance between anchoring and exploration, with evolutionary implications for tail fiber design and infection efficiency.
